body:
What is quantum entanglement?

Quantum entanglement is a phenomenon in which 2 or more quantum systems share a joint quantum state that cannot be expressed as a product of individual-system states or a statistical mixture of such products.

Entanglement is an important resource in quantum information science. It allows quantum systems to exhibit correlations that cannot, in general, be explained using ordinary independent states or classical shared randomness.

When qubits are entangled, their measurement outcomes can be related even when the qubits are physically separated. The exact relationship depends on the particular entangled state and the measurement performed.

Understanding entanglement through 2 qubits

Consider a specially prepared entangled pair of qubits, A and B. If both qubits are measured in the same computational basis, suppose the prepared state produces these results:

  • Both qubits are measured as 0, giving the combined result 00, with probability 50%.
  • Both qubits are measured as 1, giving the combined result 11, with probability 50%.
  • The combined results 01 and 10 do not occur in this ideal preparation when both qubits are measured in that basis.

If qubit A is measured as 0, the corresponding measurement of qubit B in the same basis will be 0. If A is measured as 1, B will be 1.

Neither observer can choose whether the result will be 0 or 1. Each individual outcome is random, but the 2 results are correlated.

This particular preparation is an example of an entangled Bell state. Other entangled states can produce different relationships, including opposite outcomes under appropriate same-basis measurements.

Entanglement compared with independent random bits

Suppose 2 classical bits are generated independently and each has an equal probability of being 0 or 1. The 4 combined results occur with equal probabilities:

  • 00: 25%
  • 01: 25%
  • 10: 25%
  • 11: 25%

In the entangled example above, only 00 and 11 occur, each with probability 50%, when measured in the specified basis.

This comparison illustrates a correlation, but an important qualification is necessary: 2 ordinary classical bits deliberately prepared with matching values can also produce only 00 and 11.

Therefore, matching outcomes in a single measurement basis do not, by themselves, prove entanglement. The genuinely quantum distinction is revealed by the full pattern of correlations obtained using suitable different measurements.

Can entanglement transmit information instantly?

Entanglement does not permit controllable communication faster than light.

Suppose 2 observers share an entangled pair and move apart. When they measure their respective qubits, they can later compare the results and discover the predicted correlations.

However, neither observer can control the random result of an individual measurement to encode an intended message. The observer receiving only their own measurement results cannot determine a message chosen by the distant observer.

To compare their results or communicate usable information, the observers still need an ordinary classical communication channel, which cannot exceed the speed-of-light limit.

Entanglement creates quantum correlations, not an instantaneous messaging system. Correlation between measurement results must not be confused with the ability to send a controlled signal.

How entanglement differs from superposition

FeatureSuperpositionEntanglement
Basic meaningCoherent combination of basis statesJoint state not expressible as a product of individual states or a statistical mixture of such products
Number of systemsPossible for 1 qubitRequires at least 2 quantum subsystems
Main characteristicQuantum amplitudes and interferenceNonclassical relationships between subsystems
Role in computingSupports coherent processingSupports joint quantum processing and correlations

A single qubit can be in superposition, but it cannot be entangled with itself as a separate qubit. Similarly, 2 qubits can each be in superposition without being entangled with one another.

Entanglement is a property of the relationship between quantum subsystems, whereas superposition describes the coherent structure of a quantum state.

Applications of entanglement

Entanglement is useful in several areas of quantum information science:

  • Quantum computing: Entangled qubits can participate in operations involving a joint quantum state, helping suitable quantum algorithms process information in ways unavailable to independent classical bits.
  • Quantum communication: Entanglement can support protocols for distributing and verifying quantum information.
  • Quantum key distribution: Certain communication protocols use entangled states to help establish shared secret encryption keys and detect disturbances associated with attempted interception.
  • Quantum teleportation: Shared entanglement, together with classical communication, can transfer an unknown quantum state between systems. It does not transport matter or permit faster-than-light messages.

These uses do not imply that every quantum communication system relies on entanglement. Some quantum key distribution methods use individually prepared quantum states instead.

Prelims focus

  • Entanglement is a property of the joint quantum state of 2 or more subsystems.
  • A single isolated qubit may be in superposition but is not entangled with a separate qubit unless such a relationship exists.
  • An entangled pair may produce correlated measurement outcomes.
  • Entanglement does not enable faster-than-light communication.
  • Quantum communication and quantum computing are distinct applications of quantum principles.
  • Trap: Correlation alone does not prove entanglement; ordinary classical systems can also have correlated results.

[Sources: IBM Quantum Learning, 'Basics of Quantum Information', 'Multiple Systems: Quantum Information', section 'Entangled States', consulted 5 November 2026; IBM Quantum Learning, 'Basics of Quantum Information', 'Entanglement in Action: Introduction', section 'Entanglement as a Resource', consulted 5 November 2026; IBM Quantum Learning, 'Quantum Mechanics Basics', section 'Entangle the Qubits', consulted 5 November 2026; National Institute of Standards and Technology, 'Quantum Computing Explained', discussion of entanglement, consulted 5 November 2026.]

body:
The basic operation of a quantum computer

A quantum computer performs computations by preparing qubits in chosen quantum states, applying controlled quantum operations and measuring the resulting states to obtain classical information.

The essential steps can be understood without studying the engineering details of a quantum processor.

Step 1: Preparing the qubits

A computation begins by preparing qubits in a known initial state. For example, the qubits may be initialized so that measurement would produce 0.

Known initial conditions allow later operations to act on a predictable starting state.

Step 2: Applying quantum operations

The quantum computer applies operations called quantum gates. These operations change the quantum states of qubits.

Depending on the intended computation, an operation may create a superposition, change the relative phases of state components or establish entanglement between qubits.

Some operations act on individual qubits, while others act jointly on more than 1 qubit. The sequence of operations is called a quantum circuit.

This use of the word circuit is a way of describing the logical sequence of quantum operations. It should not be confused with an ordinary electric circuit containing only wires, switches and conventional electronic components.

Step 3: Using interference and quantum correlations

After the initial preparation, the computer manipulates the quantum state according to its algorithm.

The algorithm may use both superposition and entanglement. Quantum interference then helps alter the probabilities of the possible final measurement results.

For a successful algorithm, the operations must be arranged so that useful outcomes become sufficiently likely to be observed.

This is the central distinction between creating a large superposition and performing a meaningful quantum computation. A large number of possible basis states does not automatically identify the correct answer.

Step 4: Measuring the final state

At the end of the computation, selected qubits are measured. A computational-basis measurement produces classical 0 or 1 values.

For example, measuring a 2-qubit register returns 1 of the 4 possible strings: 00, 01, 10 or 11.

The computer does not return every component of the quantum superposition as a separate readable result.

When the result is probabilistic, the computation may be repeated many times to estimate how frequently different outputs occur. The results can then be interpreted using ordinary classical computation.

Why a quantum computer is not automatically faster

A quantum register can represent a superposition involving many basis combinations, but this does not make every computational problem easy.

To obtain a useful result, a quantum algorithm must take advantage of the mathematical structure of the problem. Its operations must produce an informative result without requiring an impractically large number of measurements.

For many everyday computational tasks, classical computers remain more suitable. Quantum computing is expected to be valuable primarily for selected problems with appropriate quantum algorithms.

The challenge of maintaining quantum states

Qubits are sensitive to unwanted interactions with their surroundings. Temperature variations, electromagnetic disturbances and other environmental effects can disrupt the state used for computation.

The loss of useful quantum coherence through interaction with the environment is called decoherence.

Decoherence and imperfect operations can introduce errors into calculations. Consequently, producing a reliable result requires the quantum state to remain sufficiently well controlled while the relevant operations are performed.

Researchers develop methods to reduce errors and protect quantum information. A larger number of physical qubits alone does not guarantee a more reliable or more useful computer.

Superposition provides possible state combinations; entanglement provides joint quantum relationships; interference helps select useful measurement probabilities. Measurement finally converts the quantum information into a classical result.

Quantum computing and classical computing work together

A practical quantum-computing task usually includes ordinary classical processing. Classical systems can specify the problem, select operations, process measurement results and interpret the output.

Therefore, quantum computing is better understood as a possible additional computing capability for suitable problems, not as an inevitable replacement for conventional computers.

Prelims focus

  • Quantum gates manipulate quantum states.
  • A quantum circuit describes a sequence of quantum operations.
  • Superposition, entanglement and interference can all contribute to quantum computation.
  • Measurement produces a classical result from a quantum state.
  • Decoherence is the disruption of useful quantum coherence through environmental interactions.
  • Trap: A larger qubit count does not automatically mean greater useful computing performance.

[Sources: IBM Quantum Learning, 'Quantum Mechanics Basics', sections on gates, entanglement and measurement, consulted 5 November 2026; IBM Quantum Learning, 'Build and Run Your First Quantum Program', discussion of measurement results and repeated runs, consulted 5 November 2026; National Institute of Standards and Technology, 'Quantum Computing Explained', sections on quantum processing, limitations and qubit fragility, consulted 5 November 2026.]

title: How Quantum Computers Process Information and Produce Results

body:
What is quantum advantage?

Quantum advantage refers to a situation in which a quantum computer performs a specified computational task better than an appropriate classical-computing method, according to a clearly defined measure of performance.

The comparison may concern computation time, computational resources, accuracy at a given cost or another suitable measure. The task and the basis of comparison must be specified.

A claim of quantum advantage does not mean that quantum computers are faster than classical computers for every problem.

Quantum computing is valuable when a suitable algorithm can exploit quantum behaviour to perform a particular computation more effectively.

Why quantum advantage is task-specific

Classical computers are extremely effective at many tasks, including document processing, web browsing, ordinary calculations and running most existing software.

Quantum computers do not automatically improve these tasks simply because they use superposition or entanglement.

A quantum advantage can exist for one carefully defined computation while a classical computer remains superior for many other computations.

Consequently, the statement that a quantum computer is faster is incomplete unless the computational task and comparison are identified.

How quantum advantage should be evaluated

A meaningful comparison requires the same computational problem to be addressed under suitable conditions.

  • Specified task: The calculation or problem must be clearly defined.
  • Classical comparison: Quantum performance must be compared with an appropriate and sufficiently efficient classical method.
  • Performance measure: The claimed advantage must identify what is improved, such as time or resource requirements.
  • Accuracy and reliability: The results must meet the accuracy required for the task.
  • Practical usefulness: An advantage on a specialised benchmark does not automatically establish usefulness for ordinary scientific or commercial work.

Claims of quantum advantage can change when researchers discover more effective classical algorithms. Therefore, experimental superiority on a particular benchmark should not be treated as permanent proof that all classical methods are inferior.

Applications where quantum computing may help

1. Simulation of molecules and materials

Molecules and materials obey the laws of quantum mechanics. Accurately predicting the behaviour of complex quantum systems can be difficult for classical computers.

A sufficiently capable quantum computer may simulate selected quantum systems more efficiently, helping researchers investigate molecular properties, chemical reactions and new materials.

Such capabilities may eventually contribute to drug discovery, materials science and chemical research. However, these are potential applications; their practical value depends on achieving adequate computational accuracy and scale.

2. Optimization problems

Optimization means selecting a good or best solution from a set of possible alternatives while satisfying specified conditions.

Examples include selecting efficient routes, assigning resources and scheduling complex activities.

Certain quantum methods are being investigated for such problems. Nevertheless, quantum advantage is not guaranteed for optimization in general. Many optimization problems have highly effective classical solutions.

3. Cryptography and cybersecurity

Cryptography protects information through mathematical techniques. Some widely used public-key cryptographic systems depend on mathematical problems that are difficult for classical computers to solve at sufficiently large sizes.

A sufficiently powerful and reliable future quantum computer could solve certain such mathematical problems much more efficiently, threatening some existing public-key cryptographic methods.

This risk has encouraged the development of post-quantum cryptography, which uses cryptographic algorithms designed to resist known quantum-computing attacks while running on conventional digital computers.

Post-quantum cryptography must be distinguished from quantum key distribution, which uses physical quantum systems to help distribute secret keys.

The existence of today's quantum processors does not mean they can already break every modern encryption system.

4. Scientific research

Quantum computing may assist selected calculations in physics, chemistry and materials research. These fields often involve interacting quantum particles whose behaviour becomes increasingly difficult to simulate exactly as systems grow.

Quantum computers may also provide specialised methods for studying quantum phenomena that are difficult to reproduce with ordinary computing techniques.

Possible application versus established advantage

AreaPossible contributionImportant qualification
Molecules and materialsSimulation of quantum behaviourRequires sufficient accuracy and computational capability
OptimizationMore efficient solutions for selected problemsNo universal advantage over classical methods
CryptographyEfficient solution of certain mathematical problemsMajor practical threats require sufficiently capable quantum computers
Scientific researchSpecialised simulations and calculationsBenefits depend on the task and available algorithms

Distinguishing the concept from the technology

Quantum advantage is a performance claim, not a physical component or a government programme.

A quantum computer is a computing system. A qubit is its basic quantum-information unit. Superposition, entanglement and interference are quantum phenomena. Quantum advantage describes superior performance on a specified task when it has been demonstrated under an appropriate comparison.

National programmes that support quantum technology aim to develop scientific and technical capabilities. Their funding, objectives or qubit targets do not themselves prove that quantum advantage has been achieved.

A demonstration of quantum advantage on a specialised benchmark is not the same as a demonstration of useful advantage across everyday applications. The task, comparison and practical relevance must be considered separately.

Prelims focus

  • Quantum advantage means superior performance on a specified task under an appropriate comparison.
  • Quantum advantage is not a claim that quantum computers are universally faster.
  • Quantum simulation is a major potential application in chemistry and materials science.
  • Quantum optimization is a research area, not a guaranteed improvement for every optimization problem.
  • Post-quantum cryptography runs on conventional computers and is distinct from quantum key distribution.
  • Trap: More qubits or a successful benchmark alone do not establish broad practical quantum advantage.

[Sources: National Institute of Standards and Technology, 'Quantum Computing Explained', discussion of potential applications, quantum advantage and limitations of benchmark demonstrations, consulted 5 November 2026; IBM Quantum Learning, 'Basics of Quantum Information', overview of quantum information and algorithms, consulted 5 November 2026; Department of Science and Technology, 'National Quantum Mission (NQM)', mission objectives and application areas, consulted 5 November 2026.]
